title: Atomic KV swap orchestration and prefetch hinting for GPU paging
creator: Asha Patel
description:
Goal: implement a coordinated, low-latency mechanism for atomically swapping KV cache pages between GPU resident slabs and host/staging memory while exposing workload-driven prefetch hints to minimize tail latency during continuous batching. This ticket captures the design, prototype, testing plan and rollout steps for an orchestration layer that ensures correctness under concurrent inference (multiple request lanes), keeps GPU kernels preemptable, and avoids OOM/oversubscription under bursty workloads.

Background: our current paged/blocked KV cache design enables oversubscription but exhibits elevated 95/99p latency during sudden sequence length spikes and when mixed batch sizes contend for the same GPU slab. Existing slab allocator work reduces fragmentation but we still see high-copy churn and inefficient prefetch behavior when the runtime decides to migrate pages.

Design highlights and decisions made so far:
- Atomic swap unit: 64KB page blocks (configurable) will be the atomic eviction/pinning granularity. This aligns with our continuous batching boundaries and reduces metadata overhead compared to per-embedding row approaches.
- Two-phase swap protocol: (1) Mark-and-reserve: runtime marks target page blocks for eviction and allocates a transient slot in the staging ring buffer; (2) Swap-commit: issue async CUDA memcpy (GPU->pinned host or secondary GPU) and update page table pointer atomically with a single CAS on a 64-bit descriptor. This avoids any transient states visible to inference threads.
- Lockless descriptor updates: use a descriptor word that encodes residency, epoch, and CRC-lite. Readers use double-read validation to avoid locks. Writers update via compare-and-swap ensuring atomic visibility.
- Prefetch hint API: a lightweight per-request hint vector passed through the scheduler that lists upcoming token offsets likely to be accessed (derived from prefix length and sampling distribution). Hints are translated into priority prefetch work items that are scheduled when GPU utilization has slack.
- Staging paths: support pinned-host staging and peer-GPU staging for Dedicated clusters with P2P. Strategy favors P2P when available to avoid host copies. A bounded staging pool prevents unbounded pinned memory growth.
- Integration with continuous batching: batching coordinator tags batch lanes with urgency scores; urgent lanes bypass background prefetch backlog and trigger immediate prefetch for hot pages. Non-urgent batches are served from best-effort cached pages or CPU-staged pages with a soft-fallback model.
- Backpressure and graceful degradation: when staging pool saturated or mem pressure high, runtime reduces max batch size for non-urgent lanes and falls back to smaller, latency-friendlier kernels.

Trade-offs considered:
- Smaller page size reduces copied bytes but increases metadata operations and CAS frequency; 64KB chosen after microbenchmarks (see artifacts) as midpoint.
- Eager prefetch increases memory usage but reduces tail latency; we implement adaptive prefetch thresholds based on observed hit-rate and GPU occupancy.
- Strong atomicity vs throughput: double-read validation adds ~5% read overhead but prevents race-induced retries under heavy contention. This was acceptable per throughput tests.

Prototype status and benchmarks:
- Prototype implemented on a feature branch: github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/724
- Microbenchmarks: synthetic multi-lane workload with 128B->8kB token distributions shows 35% reduction in 99p latency versus baseline under bursty arrivals when prefetch enabled. Detailed numbers in the design doc.

Testing and validation plan:
- Unit tests for descriptor CAS and double-read validation (simulated races on CPU).
- Integration tests: multi-lane continuous batching harness with configurable prefetch hints and staged P2P host fallback.
- Fault injection: simulate mid-swap GPU OOM and staged memcpy failures to validate rollback and retry semantics.
- Perf benchmarks: end-to-end TTF (time-to-first-token) and 95/99p gen latency across seq lengths [256,1024,4096] and batch mixes.

Rollout plan:
- Canary rollout to dedicated pool with non-critical tenants (10% traffic) for 2 weeks with metrics: 99p latency, staging pool usage, memcpy bandwidth, and CAS retry count.
- If stable, enable for another 30% of traffic and collect production telemetry.
- Full rollout gated on minimal regression (no >5% increase in P50 or >10% in GPU memory usage) and SLO compliance.

Open questions / risks:
- Descriptor size: 64-bit may limit future fields; if more metadata required we need a secondary metadata table with indirection which complicates atomicity.
- Prefetch accuracy: poor prefetch heuristics can waste staging memory; need to allocate budget and decay policy.
- Cross-GPU eviction thrashing in multi-tenant hosts; may need tenant-aware reservations or cooperative eviction.

Next steps:
- Finalize staging pool allocator (Liam) and implement bounded queueing for prefetch work (Fran).
- Add deterministic race tests and increase CI coverage.
- Prepare canary dashboard panels in Console: kv-prefetch-hit, swap-latency, staging-occupancy, CAS-retries.

Files / artifacts:
- Design doc: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/RUNTIME/atomic-kv-swap-design
- Prototype PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/724
- Benchmark scripts: https://drive.redwood.ai/drive/folders/kv-swap-microbench

Acceptance criteria:
1) Atomically visible page swaps with no observed race corruption under stress tests.
2) 99p generation latency reduced >=20% vs baseline in mixed-batch benchmarks where prefetch budget is non-zero.
3) No unbounded growth in pinned host memory; staging pool enforced.
4) Canary rollout shows no SLO violations for affected tenants.
